text: Opening and the greatness of Vayu. As the revered Lord भगवान् धन्वन्तरि spoke, now therefore we shall explain the diagnosis of the diseases caused by Vata (वातव्याधिनिदानम्) in the opening of the text. (v. 1-2) Sushruta, having approached the feet of Dhanvantari—who is the best among the maintainers of dharma (धर्मभृतां वरिष्ठम्) and originated from nectar (अमृतोद्भवम्)—asks him. (v. 3) Sushruta asks the best among speakers to tell him the seat, function, and diseases of Vayu, both in its normal state (प्रकृतिभूतस्य) and when vitiated by aggravating factors (व्यापन्नस्य च कोपनैः). (v. 4) The best of physicians, having heard that speech, spoke, identifying this revered Vayu as self-born (स्वयम्भू). (v. 5) Because of independence (स्वातन्त्र्यात्), eternal existence (नित्यभावात्), and being all-pervading (सर्वगत्वात्), Vayu is indeed the soul of all (सर्वात्मा) and is bowed to by all worlds (सर्वलोकनमस्कृतः). (v. 6)

Nature, qualities and functions of Vayu. Vayu is the unmanifest yet manifestly active cause behind the origin, maintenance, and destruction of beings, possessing the physical qualities of being dry (रूक्ष), cold, light, and rough (v. 7). It moves horizontally, is twofold, is abundant in rajas, possesses inconceivable potency, and acts as the leader of the doshas and the king of disease-groups (v. 8). Vayu moves swiftly and repeatedly, and its primary abodes in the body are the pakvadhana (large intestine) and the guda (anus) (v. 9). When it is unprovoked (अकुपितः अनिलः), Vayu maintains the equilibrium of doshas, dhatus, and agnis, ensures the proper perception of sensory objects, and promotes the regularity of all bodily functions (v. 10).

The five Vayus: seats, actions, disorders. Just as a single fire is divided into five ways by names, sites, and functions, a single wind (वात:) is similarly divided into five types (v. 11). These five winds—प्राणः, उदानः, समानः, व्यानः, and अपानः—staying in their respective places, maintain the embodied living being (v. 12). Prana moves in the mouth, acting as the sustainer of the body, causing food to enter inside and supporting life-breaths (v. 13). Udana is the best among winds that goes upwards, and when vitiated, mostly produces diseases like hiccup and dyspnoea (v. 14). It manifests special varieties of speech and song, and specially causes diseases located above the collarbone (v. 15). Samana moves in the stomach and intestines (आमपक्वाशयचरः) united with the digestive fire, digests food, and separates its specific essences (v. 16). Vyana moves in the entire body, is engaged in circulating nutrient fluid (रससंवहनोद्यतः), and causes diseases such as gulma, agnisada, and atisara (v. 17). It also causes the discharge of sweat and blood, moves in five ways, and when aggravated mostly creates diseases spreading throughout the entire body (v. 18). Apana has the large intestine as its abode and at the proper time draws downwards faeces, urine, semen, foetus, and menstrual blood (v. 19). When aggravated, it produces terrible diseases residing in the bladder and rectum, while disorders of semen and prameha are born from the aggravation of vyana and apana (v. 20). If these winds residing in various locations are simultaneously aggravated, they would undoubtedly destroy the body, after which the author will speak further (v. 21).

Vayu lodged in organs and tissues. In the Sushruta Samhita Nidana Sthana, Acharya Sushruta explains the specific disorders caused by aggravated वायु (Vayu) when it lodges in different organs and tissues. Aggravated Vayu in the आमाशये (stomach) produces vomiting and other diseases (v. 22). Located in the पक्वाशय (colon), it causes delusion, fainting, thirst, cardiac constriction, flank pain, intestinal gurgling, and navel colic (v. 23). When aggravated, it causes difficulty in urination and defecation, abdominal distension, sacral pain, and impairment of the sense organs in the ears and elsewhere (v. 24). Seated in the त्वक् (skin), it causes discoloration, throbbing, dryness, numbness, tingling, pricking pain, and cracking or bursting of the skin (v. 25). Situated in the blood, it produces painful lumps and ulcers, while in the fat it causes lumps with mild pain and no ulcers (v. 26). Reaching the veins, it causes pain and vein contraction and filling; reaching the ligaments, it causes stiffness, tremor, pain, and convulsion (v. 27). Located in the joints, it destroys them with pain and swelling, and in the bones, it causes bone wasting, piercing pain, and sharp pain (v. 28). When residing in the bone marrow, the pain never subsides, and in the semen, it leads to either absence of emission or excessive discharge (v. 29). The all-pervading Vayu successively moves about the hands, feet, head, and tissues, or pervades the entire body (v. 30). Finally, when this all-pervading Vayu is mixed with other doshas in the aforesaid sites, it produces mixed diseases characterized by stiffness, convulsion, numbness, swelling, and pain (v. 31).

Vata joined with or covered by other doshas. When the aggravated मारुतः (Vayu) reaches various parts of the body, it causes numerous diseases, and when combined with पित्त (Pitta), it produces burning sensation, heat, and fainting (v. 32). When Vayu is covered by कफ (Kapha), it causes coldness, swelling, heaviness, pricking pain like with needles, aversion to touch, and numbness (v. 33). When Maruta is combined with शोणित (blood), remaining Pitta disorders occur, and when प्राण (Prana vayu) is covered with Pitta, vomiting and burning sensation arise (v. 34). When उदान (Udana vayu) is combined with Pitta and covered by Kapha, weakness, languor, drowsiness, discoloration, fainting, burning sensation, dizziness, and exhaustion arise (v. 35). When समान (Samana vayu) is covered by Kapha and combined with Pitta, there is absence of sweat, lack of horripilation, weak digestive fire, coldness, and stiffness, along with sweating, burning sensation, heat, and fainting (v. 36). When अपान (Apana vayu) is combined with Pitta and covered by Kapha, there occur increased feces and urine, horripilation, burning sensation and heat, and असृग्दर (menorrhagia or bleeding disorder) (v. 37). When व्यान (Vyana vayu) is covered by Kapha, heaviness of the lower body occurs, and when covered by Pitta, burning sensation, tossing of the limbs, and exhaustion happen (v. 38). When Vyana vata is enveloped by Kapha, all limbs feel heavy along with stiffness of the bones, joints, and physical movements (v. 39).

Vatarakta: causes, signs and prognosis. Vatarakta is primarily caused in tender persons who indulge in improper diet and regimen, and who suffer excessive strain from disease, travel, women, wine, and exercise (v. 40). It is further aggravated by the reversal of seasonal suitability, errors in oleation, lack of exercise or coitus, obesity, riding vehicles like elephants, horses, and camels, and excessive consumption of sharp, hot, sour, alkaline, and vegetable foods alongside heat (v. 41-42). This causes quick vitiation of blood, which obstructs the path of aggravated wind, and in turn intensely vitiates the blood even more (v. 43). Combined with vitiated wind and its predominance, it is called Vatarakta, just as blood combined with vitiated Pitta or Kapha results in similar manifestations (v. 44). Vatarakta in the feet causes aversion to touch, pricking and splitting pain, excessive dryness, numbness, severe burning, extreme heat, and soft red swellings (v. 45). When vitiated by Kapha, the feet become itchy, white, cold, swollen, thick, and stiff, while the combination of all doshas shows the composite features of each (v. 46). The premonitory stage presents looseness, sweating, coldness, perversion, discoloration, pricking pain, numbness, heaviness, and burning (v. 47). Like poison, it originates at the base of the feet and sometimes hands, spreading through the body (v. 48). It is incurable when it bursts up to the knee, ulcerates, oozes, and is afflicted by complications like muscle and vitality wasting, or when vitiated Vata pervades all channels, whereas a one-year-old condition is manageable (v. 49-50).

Convulsions, spasms and rigidity. When the aggravated moving वायु quickly jerks the body repeatedly, the condition is designated as आक्षेपक (Aksepaka) (v. 51). If वायु associated with कफ stays intensely in those sites and repeatedly causes the patient to fall, it is named अपतानक (Apatanaka) (v. 52). A painful variant called दण्डापतानक (Dandapatanaka) makes the patient stiff like a staff and causes excessive stiffness of the jaw with great difficulty in consuming food (v. 53). When the patient bends like a bow, the condition located in the fingers, ankles, abdomen, heart, chest, and throat is called धनुःस्तम्भ (Dhanurstambha) (v. 54). When a powerful wind agitates the network of tendons, the patient has fixed eyes, a stiff jaw, broken sides, and is vomiting phlegm (v. 55). A strong मारुत (Vata) causes inward bending when it bends a human being inwards like a bow (v. 56), whereas residing in the network of external tendons, it causes external bending and breaks the chest, waist, and thighs, which wise men declare to be incurable (v. 57). Finally, आक्षेपक can be produced by वायु associated with कफ and पित्त, by वायु alone, or as a fourth type caused by अभिघात (trauma) (v. 58), and any अपतानक caused by abortion, excessive bleeding, and trauma is not curable (v. 59).

Hemiplegia, Apatantraka, stiff neck. When the excessively aggravated wind (मातरिश्वा) travels downwards, obliquely, and to the upper body, it enters the channels (धमनीः) (v. 60). By loosening the ligamentous bindings of the joints of one side of the body, it strikes that side, which expert physicians call hemiplegia or पक्षाघात (v. 61). When afflicted by Vata, the entire half of the body becomes functionless and devoid of sensation, causing the patient to either fall down or lose their life (v. 62). Physicians know that पक्षाघात caused purely by Vata is extremely difficult to cure (कृच्छ्रसाध्यतमम्), that which is combined with another dosha is curable (साध्यम्), and that which is caused by tissue depletion (क्षयहेतुकम्) is incurable (असाध्यम्) (v. 63). 

When aggravated Vayu moves upwards from its own place, it afflicts the heart, head, and temples, causing bodily convulsions and bending (v. 64). The patient may have closed or stiff eyes, remain motionless, experience breathlessness or breathe with difficulty, lose consciousness, and moan (v. 65). When the heart is released the patient becomes normal, but when it is obstructed they faint, which should be known as अपतन्त्रक caused by Vata associated with Kapha (v. 66). Indeed, that same Vayu, when covered by Kapha and provoked by daytime sleep, sitting, standing, and gazing at an open path, produces stiffness of the neck or मन्यास्तम्भ (v. 67).

Facial palsy. Excessive loud speaking, eating hard things, laughing, yawning, lifting heavy burdens, or maintaining an uneven bed act as the causes that provoke the wind (वायु) (v. 68). Therefore, the wind (अनिलः), having reached the joints of the head, nose, lips, chin, forehead, and eyes, and having afflicted the face, produces the disease named अर्दितम् (Ardita) (v. 69). Half of the face becomes crooked, the neck also turns away, the head shakes, and there is obstruction of speech along with abnormalities of the eyes and other parts (v. 70). On that side, there is pain in the neck, chin, and teeth, with horripilation as the foremost symptom, along with tremor and a turbid eye (v. 71). Experts in diseases call that disease अर्दितम् (Arditam) in which the wind (वायुः) moving upwards in the skin causes numbness (स्वापः), pricking pain (स्तोदः), and stiffness of the neck and jaw (मन्याहनुग्रहः) (v. 72). The disease अर्दितम् (arditam) is not curable if it is of three years' duration, or if it occurs in a person who is emaciated, has unblinking eyes, speaks with slurred speech, and is trembling (v. 73).

Disorders of limbs, senses and abdomen. Acharya Sushruta first explains that when the tendon of the heel and toes is afflicted by the aggravated अनिल, it restricts leg movement, a condition known as गृध्रसी (v. 74). Similarly, when the tendon of the palm and fingers from the back of the arm causes a loss of function in both arms, it is known as विश्वाची (v. 75). A severe, painful swelling in the middle of the knee that resembles the head of a jackal is caused by वातशोणित (v. 76). When वायु located in the hip affects the thigh tendon, it causes lameness called खञ्ज, and if both thighs are impaired, it results in पङ्गु (v. 77). A person who trembles and limps while walking with loosened joint-connections suffers from कलायखञ्ज (v. 78), while pain in the ankle caused by uneven foot placement is recognized as वातकण्टक (v. 79). 

When अनिल combined with पित्त and blood produces a burning sensation in the feet that worsens with walking, it is designated as पाददाह (v. 80), whereas a tingling, sleep-like numbness in the feet caused by aggravated कफ and वात is called पादहर्ष (v. 81). When वायु localizes in the shoulder region, drying up the ligament and contracting the blood vessels, it produces अवबाहुक (v. 82). Deafness (बाधिर्य) occurs when pure or कफ-associated वायु obstructs the sound-carrying channels (v. 83), and earache (कर्णशूल) happens when the wind causes a piercing pain through the lower jaw, temples, head, and neck into the ears (v. 84). Furthermore, sound-carrying channels covered by कफ-associated वायु can render a person motionless, mute, or cause nasal and stuttering speech (v. 85). 

Downward-moving pain arising from the seats of feces and urine and piercing the गुद and उपस्थ is termed तूनी (v. 86), and when that same pain moves upward with force toward the पक्वाशय, it is known as प्रतितूनी (v. 87). Terrible आध्मान refers to abdominal distension with rumbling and severe pain arising from the obstruction of वात (v. 88), while प्रत्याध्मान arises from the stomach with freed sides and heart when the wind is agitated by कफ (v. 89). Finally, a dense, stone-like, elevated mass obstructing outer passages is known as वाताष्ठीला (v. 90), and when this same painful condition arises obliquely in the abdomen to obstruct flatus, feces, and urine, it is called प्रत्यष्ठीला (v. 91).
